maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES ALLEGED MISLEADING OF PARLIAMENT    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was quite interested in the statement made this afternoon by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, particularly because of the minister's failure to come to grips with the subject matter of the motion presented to this house this afternoon. During the time the Minister of Trade and Commerce was speaking I took notes, and I failed to find any reference to the_ point at issue at this time. He drew a red herring across the trail by going into a discussion of Westcoast Transmission Company.

I was greatly interested in what he had to say on that score, and I want to assure him that I will read his remarks tomorrow when I receive Hansard because, as Your Honor knows, we hold no brief for West-coast Transmission Company nor for any other privately-owned pipe-line company in this country. I think it is an extremely poor argument indeed to suggest that because Westcoast Transmission Company undertook certain procedures, the very fact that that was done absolves Trans-Canada Pipe Lines of any blame in connection with anything they have done. I think the minister's argument would tend to suggest that he believes that two wrongs make a right.
When the specific allegation is made that there was something improper in the way this matter was handled he seems to suggest that because some other pipe-line company does business in a certain way, that fact in some way excuses the actions taken by himself with regard to the matter now before the house. It seems to me that the sum total of the argument presented by the Minister of Trade and Commerce was that since some Other pipe-line company was a worse offender than Trans-Canada Pipe Lines, therefore that fact absolves Trans-Canada Pipe Lines or the government of any blame in this connection.
It seems to me that the argument presented by the Minister of Trade and Commerce this afternoon points out more clearly than anything else the need for public ownership of pipe lines in this country. There is only one way in which the interests of the general public can be guaranteed, and that is through public ownership. I think this whole debate will point out that one inescapable fact. If nothing else comes of this discussion we have had this afternoon, I think it will impress upon the Canadian people the fact that the only way in which their interests can be protected is when they themselves, through their government, have the ownership and control of these carriers which are so essential in this modern day.
The minister on former occasions has made certain references to the role of some of the gentlemen who have been prominently mentioned this afternoon. He also spoke of the need for these options as a means of providing some incentive for men at the top to put forth their best effort. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the options we have been discussing thus far in this debate are certainly not designed to create any selfreliance or further initiative on the part of the gentlemen concerned. We know that the president of the company had one share in his name. It was brought to our attention
Trans-Canada Pipe Lines this afternoon-indeed we knew it from the debate of ten months ago-that there was some other person of the same surname on the list of shareholders. But I suggest that fact is immaterial. The fact of the matter is that the president of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines owned one $8 share. Hence when we hear the tearful stories about all these tremendous risks encountered in this particular venture, we have to bear those facts in mind.
We heard some reference to the worry and the anxiety. I dare say there was a certain amount of worry and anxiety. I suppose some of that anxiety was removed when the government decided to grant a loan of $80 million of the taxpayers' money, because after they received the charter they sat there on their haunches and did nothing until 1956. Even when the initial proposals to build the northern Ontario section were made in an effort to get some action out of this company, they were even then not prepared to go ahead. Apparently the only way the government were able to persuade them to go ahead with this venture was when they promised to lend them the money to build the western leg of the line. Worry and anxiety about whether the government would lend them the $80 million is about the only type of anxiety I could see in this particular venture.
It seems to me the Minister of Trade and Commerce is selling many Canadians short when he suggests that there is a shortage of skill or a shortage of brains here in Canada, that there are only one or two people in this country who can possibly undertake a venture of this sort. I think that is an insult to a great many Canadian businessmen who I am sure are quite capable of carrying out a venture of this kind. Moreover, I suggest that any public-spirited businessman in this country would be happy to serve this country if he were called upon to aid in the building of a pipe line under public ownership. I suggest that any man who would refuse simply by virtue of the fact that, by continuing in private ownership, he hoped he might get options to purchase stock in order that he might amass a personal fortune for himself, is not the type of public-spirited man who has built up this country over the years.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the other red herring that was drawn across the path this afternoon had to do with an attempt to introduce into the debate the personal affairs of the president of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited. I do not think the personnel or the individuals concerned is an important matter. I think the principle is all-important. We had this great effort that the hon. member for Peace River presented this afternoon, when he tried to reduce us to tears over the

Trans-Canada Pipe Lines plight of this gentleman who had, to use the hon. member's own expression, "stepped down", the implication being that he was making a great personal sacrifice.
He has a salary of $35,000 a year and a retiring allowance or separation allowance or pension or whatever you want to call it of $15,000 a year for a few years after retirement, plus the option to purchase 60,000 shares of stock. Then we are told that this man is "stepping down", that he is lowering his standard of living. When a man makes more money than the Prime Minister of Canada, nevertheless we are told that he is stepping down in the economic scale in order to take on the responsibility of president of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES ALLEGED MISLEADING OF PARLIAMENT    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: What was he making previously?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES ALLEGED MISLEADING OF PARLIAMENT    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I am not in a position to say that. Perhaps our hon. friends who mentioned earlier today that some people were withholding information should have informed us as to the previous salaries. At the same time on this question of withholding information, when the hon. member for Peace River spoke this afternoon I think perhaps he might have informed us as to what salary was being received by the president of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines at the time he was president of Merrill Petroleums Limited.
This suggestion that there was a great personal sacrifice on the part of the president of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines in taking over the presidency I think will not meet a very favourable response from the people of this country. I am certain that those who have been connected with this venture have been very well rewarded indeed.
It seemed to me, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Peace River made some reference to the fact that this was only a paper gain, and that since presumably he has not disposed of the shares, actually he has not made that money. Of course the only thing standing in the way of realizing a real capital gain is the selling of the shares, and the moment he wants to put those shares on the market he will realize his gain. My suggestion is that the reason the gentleman will not put them on the market is he hopes they will go up in value.
You know, pipe lines have been very profitable undertakings. As a matter of fact the house is now considering a bill concerning Trans-Mountain pipe line. We know these shares once sold for $10 and today they are selling at around $115. The company is asking permission for a stock split. My suggestion is this, that if Trans-Canada Pipe

Lines is as successful or even if it is only half as successful as Trans-Mountain pipe line, by holding these shares the president of the company stands to make more than the $110,000 which he may realize at this moment. If these shares follow the general tendency to increase in value they might go up to $50 a share, and by holding these shares until that time the president of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines can make as high as $3 million in capital gains. I do not know what type of argument it is to say that because he has not seen fit to sell the shares, it is only a paper profit.
One statement to which the hon. member for Dauphin referred just before six o'clock was that of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to the effect that as of 2 p.m. tomorrow afternoon the government would be no longer involved in the affairs of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines. The presumption is that when he is asked a question on the orders of the day the minister will say it is no longer the concern of the government, it is a private enterprise. There are varying opinions on that. There is an editorial in the Ottawa Journal of Thursday, February 21, which I think neatly states this question in its proper perspective. The editorial is entitled, "But is it a private company?" It reads:
A ked in parliament about the transaction under which two ranking officers of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited were given options to buy tens of thousands of shares of the company's common stock (one bought 55,000 shares and the other 50,000 shares, netting them immediately an enormous paper profit) Mr. C. D. Howe described the arrangement as "nothing unusual", something "purely within a private company".
Is that right?
Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited was a private company when it started out; when it entered into an arrangement with the government under which, given a monopoly, it undertook to build a pipe line with its own money to bring Alberta gas to eastern Canada.
Did it remain a private company when having defaulted on its undertaking it begged and received money from the public treasury to carry on the work it was pledged to do on its own?
And does it remain a "private company" when at this very moment a segment of the pipe line through which northern gas will flow-that through northern Ontario-is made possible only because the dominion government and the government of Ontario put up millions of public money for Trans-Canada to do a job it had undertaken to do on its own?
The truth is that in so far as bringing Alberta gas to eastern Canada is concerned Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited would not exist at all were it not for government money; public money.
That being the record-and the record is there for all to read-Mr. Howe's statement about Trans-Canada being a "private company" free to do what it pleases to enable its directors to make money out of its common stock, seems a bit strange to say the least.
And not less strange when it is remembered that dividends on this common stock must come out of the price eastern consumers will pay for Alberta gas.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES ALLEGED MISLEADING OF PARLIAMENT    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Order; this must not be taken as a precedent, because the reading of editorials is not in accordance with our rules of debate.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES ALLEGED MISLEADING OF PARLIAMENT    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I had just concluded the reading of the editorial, Mr. Speaker. I desired to place that editorial on record because I think it sums up very neatly the proper concept. The position of the Minister of Trade and Commerce that because this loan is going to be repaid at two o'clock tomorrow the government has no further interest in Trans-Canada Pipe Lines is utter nonsense. After all, in the first negotiations leading up to the legislation being put through parliament under dictatorial methods last spring, there was no talk initially of the loan to build the western leg. We had been led to understand that the government of Ontario and the government of Canada would build the northern Ontario section, and the balance of the line would be financed by Trans-Canada Pipe Lines. Then when nothing was done they stalled around and delayed, waiting of course for their anxiety to be removed through a loan of $80 million from the public purse. The minister is certainly not going to suggest that if the loan had not been made, even at this time the government of Canada would not be interested in the future of this line.
The fact of the matter is that this pipe-line company will have a monopoly. Once the pipe line is built, and once consumers have converted to that type of energy or fuel, then the company exercises a complete monopoly. Therefore, even apart from the arrangements under which the line was built, no responsible government official could say today it is not the concern of this government what is done by this pipe-line company with respect to consumers, markets and so forth.
This afternoon the Minister of Trade and Commerce sought to create the impression that these are two separate matters. When the minister was asked about the northern Ontario section I recall he said that was separate and distinct. Is it?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES ALLEGED MISLEADING OF PARLIAMENT    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Public ownership.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES ALLEGED MISLEADING OF PARLIAMENT    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: That is the point; we argued that if Ontario and the federal government were going to build the northern Ontario section, logically and sensibly we should have built the whole line. That is the position we take.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES ALLEGED MISLEADING OF PARLIAMENT    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: You said that a year ago.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES ALLEGED MISLEADING OF PARLIAMENT    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
We said that a year ago, and we say it today. What has happened today is the best proof possible that our position was sound at that time. There could be no greater vindication of the stand which C.C.F. members took in that debate last spring than what
Trans-Canada Pipe Lines has transpired since. We have been consistent throughout in our advocacy of public ownership of this pipe line, and it appears evident today that all the fears we expressed at that time concerning the future of this pipe line, that a group of private individuals were using the building of the pipe line not primarily to provide energy to consumers in Ontario but as a means of enriching their own pockets, have been realized.
There is an essential difference, in that we maintain that the resources of this country ought to be used to the advantage of the people of Canada.
I can recall some hon. gentlemen suggesting that the pipe line is not a natural resource. That is true, but it is even more important; because whoever gets control of the pipe line has a monopoly over the transportation of that energy, and conceivably is in a position to take advantage of both the producer at one end and the consumer at the other, although we know the pipe line is controlled in large measure by the producers of gas. In other words, they control not only the sources of supply but the means whereby the gas is transported to the consumer.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what has happened since that ill-fated day when this legislation was finally passed in the House of Commons I think indicates very clearly the need for rethinking with respect to our policy toward the building of pipe lines in this country. It is clearly evident that there is only one way in which the public interest can be guaranteed and protected, and that is by public ownership.
I should like to make this comment in closing. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and my colleague from Nanaimo presented a very clear-cut case dealing with the relationship of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to this particular matter. When the Minister of Trade and Commerce got to his feet he did not answer the allegations. He led us far astray. He talked about Westcoast Transmission. He has not answered the complaints. He has not answered the criticism levelled at him this afternoon; and I would suggest to the Prime Minister, or to the Minister of Finance, that he do what the Minister of Trade and Commerce failed to do this afternoon, namely rise and give us a reasonable explanation for the conduct of the government over the last 10 months.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES ALLEGED MISLEADING OF PARLIAMENT    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I consider the time of this house valuable. That is why when I speak I just crack off what I have to say in short order. I just wonder how much this pipe-line debate has cost the taxpayers of Canada this afternoon and tonight.

Trans-Canada Pipe Lines

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES ALLEGED MISLEADING OF PARLIAMENT    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: How much money has been made out of it?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES ALLEGED MISLEADING OF PARLIAMENT    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I think the Leader of the
Opposition said a good thing-he says some good things-when he said that the pipe line was finished last year. I thought it was, but we have the pipe line through and all around this house now, Mr. Speaker, until we are sick and tired of hearing it. We heard that the pipe line was coming only to Winnipeg and that the government put up the money. The Minister of Trade and Commerce told us last year that we were not taking much risk. Tomorrow we are getting the money back at 5 per cent. If any corporation had a manager who would invest $50 million or more and make 5 per cent I know what would happen. He would get either an increase in salary or a trip to Dublin on the other side of Ireland and good wishes for the future.
I think we have heard enough about this pipe line. Let us get on with the business of the house. Thank you for your patience.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES ALLEGED MISLEADING OF PARLIAMENT    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: This is the business of the house.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES ALLEGED MISLEADING OF PARLIAMENT    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Trans-Canada Pipe Lines
At that stage Trans-Canada Pipe Lines caught on with the public of Canada and the United States, and in recent weeks the project has been successfully financed. Demand has far exceeded the supply of securities.
A good many Canadians, including myself, found that the orders which were actually filled represented only a small fraction of the stock they would like to have bought. I think, as a result of this, some artificial ideas have been created in the mind of the public about the value of this security. Mr. Speaker, I do have a tremendous faith in the long-term future of this project, and I believe that in the years ahead it is going to be profitable. I believe, also, that its shareholders will benefit. But I do know that when this pipe line is built and in operation, regardless of how successful or unsuccessful it is going to prove to the shareholders, it is going to result in some tremendous developments in the chemical and petrochemical industries in western Canada, and is going to make life a good deal easier for many hundreds of thousands of Canadians between Saskatchewan and Quebec who will have access to a new and convenient fuel for home heating.
But to return to the question of the Trans-Canada company, the issue before us is, I think, whether the minister made a mistake, whether he mislead the house. I think the answer to that is yes. Then the further question arises here today whether or not certain executives of the company have profited unduly. They have been called several different terms here today; I will not mention the names which have been applied to them, but I think it is fair to say that no one in this house who has any conception of what lies behind the building up of a project such as this would apply the kind of terms to these two gentlemen that we have heard here today.
In conclusion, sir, may I say that I believe these two gentlemen who have received options on Trans-Canada stock deserve the options they have received. They have not deserved some of the criticism which has been heaped on them today. My only regret, speaking lightly, is that I was not in a position to participate in the same kind of option myself. I think they, together with a great many others concerned in this project, have achieved something that Canada will finally appreciate.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES ALLEGED MISLEADING OF PARLIAMENT    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although the headline in the Ottawa Journal reads "Misled House, Howe Admits" only the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the hon. member for Fort William have spoken from the government side to debate this important subject.
[Mr. Nickle.l
The hon. member for Calgary South did criticize the minister for misleading the house, but the balance of his speech seemed to give a good deal of comfort to hon. members opposite. We feel that the Prime Minister, who has achieved a reputation as a very able corporation counsel, should come to the rescue of his colleague and offer something more constructive and more valuable than has been presented by the hon. member for Fort William.

Mr. Speaker, there are a few remarks that I should like to make in this debate. Actually I think some of the issues that have arisen in the discussion have been rather fundamental.
I was much interested in the speech which was made to the house by the hon. member for Calgary South. I think the hon. member perhaps did a good deal to focus our attention upon what to me are the real issues involved in the debate that has arisen. He


made some reference to the idea that, in his opinion, some of the debate had been an attempt to blast the personal reputations of a few of the officers of this Trans-Canada Pipe Lines company. In listening to that section of his remarks I felt he was dealing principally with the speech made this afternoon by his colleague the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace, who I thought went to some length in making the question of Mr. Tanner's involvement in this matter a personal issue.
However, I think in the main portion of his speech he brought the matter into what, to me, is its proper perspective, and indicated that the fact that a Mr. Tanner and certain other gentlemen happen to be involved in this debate because of their holding office in Trans-Canada Pipe Lines is really incidental. I think that point has been brought out quite clearly in some of the speeches that have been made by other C.C.F. members participating in this debate. All I should like to say is that as far as I am concerned, if people like Mr. Tanner or any others who go into the business life of this country want to play with fire, they can expect occasionally to have their hands scorched a little bit.
There are some of us who are prepared to challenge the philosophy which was inherent in the speech by the hon. member for Calgary South and in the speech made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, namely that certain practices to which they referred are right and legitimate. To me that is the real issue that is involved in this debate. As indicated by the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, it has arisen on this particular occasion because Trans-Canada Pipe Lines became directly involved in the legislation that was before this house last year. The practices carried on in connection with such things as the stock options and other related practices that the hon. member for Calgary South and the Minister of Trade and Commerce are prepared to accept as normal business practices are the practices which we are prepared directly to challenge.
As I say, it is because of the fact that Trans-Canada Pipe Lines and its actions and those of its officers became directly the property of this house through the use of public funds to assist this project that we feel it is only right and appropriate that we use this occasion to focus attention on our belief that this is the sort of practice which should not be continued in Canadian business life; that this is the sort of practice that goes to the root of some of the economic problems that are growing daily in this nation; and that in fact many of the problems that are involved

in what has been referred to as the government's tight money policy arise in part out of the fact that we have a government which is prepared to allow our economy to go on functioning with this sort of practice in it.
I was particularly interested this afternoon in certain references that were made by the hon. member for Peace River to what he called short-circuited thinking. As far as I am concerned, if any particular segment of the membership of this house have been indulging in what could be called short-circuited thinking, it is the members of the group led by the hon. member for Peace River. Time after time, Mr. Speaker, we have listened to the hon. member for Peace River and some of his colleagues get to their feet on the floor of this house and give us long dissertations on what they call in a rather vague manner putting purchasing power into the hands of the people".
They allow themselves to be completely blinded to the fact that the practice of making unearned gains from stock transactions, such as the one under discussion, is one of the most effective means used by a small minority of the people of this country, who have been able to manoeuvre into a favourable position, to withhold full purchasing power from the hands of the people.
If they are going to talk in this house and throughout the country about the idea of putting purchasing power into the hands of the people, it seems to me they had better check their own circuits for shorts, so far as their thinking is concerned. They had better get down to doing some real thinking about what is involved in putting purchasing power into the hands of the people. Every time somebody like the officer of a pipe-line company manages to short-circuit out of the purchasing stream that goes into the pockets of the average Canadian citizen the amount of money which is being short-circuited in this transaction, then the average citizen is the loser.
Occasionally the department of the Minister of Trade and Commerce issues statistics about the gross national product, the total amount of wealth that is available to the citizens throughout Canada, the wealth that is produced by the people of Canada. If we have a population of 15 million or 16 million, that wealth can only be divided so far amongst so many of us. I am not going to try to suggest what the exact amount of this gain might be, because I could not make the kind of analysis of the stock transactions of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines that was made by the hon. member for Calgary South, but every time $50,000 or $100,000 or $500,000 is taken out of the purchasing stream by this sort
Trans-Canada Pipe Lines of transaction, then you are reducing the purchasing power that can go into the hands of the old age pensioners or the wage earners of this country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES ALLEGED MISLEADING OF PARLIAMENT    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
There are one or two things I should like to add to this debate before the question is put. I shall be as brief as possible. Clearly there are two fundamental misapprehensions on the part of hon. members who have seen fit to support the proposal placed before the house by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. The first is that the action of this parliament in approving the legislation which provided a loan to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines in some way eliminated all risk that was attendant upon that project.
The hon. member for Calgary South has dealt with that aspect of the matter. I think it should be underlined that any action taken by this parliament was not intended or

designed to eliminate any risk that was being run by anybody who was putting risk capital in this venture, or who was connected with it from that point of view. The risks of the venture were all still there. All this parliament did was to make it possible for the project to proceed in a way that enabled the company to make the necessary purchase and sale contracts for gas that eventually made the project financeable. Those in this house who opposed the loan proposals last year were not opposing something that would expose the taxpayers, or the public purse, to risk. They were opposing the only feasible method at that time which could get the pipe line started and put the company in a position to finance itself, and for that reason they were opposing the building of the pipe line itself and nothing else.
The second misconception that underlies the attitude particularly of the C.C.F. party is that what was put up by way of a loan was in some way providing risk capital for this project. Mr. Speaker, nothing of course could be farther from the fact. The loan that was provided and which was drawn upon by Trans-Canada Pipe Lines during the course of the construction of the western section this year was a fully secured loan, secured by a first mortgage on the entire undertaking of the company. It was a loan at a fixed rate of interest of 5 per cent, and it was not in any respect risk capital, nor was the government or the taxpayer of Canada participating in this company in a way which was intended to give the public treasury any investment in the company which would participate either in the eventual profits of the company or in the risk of loss. The fact is that, as has already been pointed out, this loan, fully secured as it was, is now to be repaid with interest and with all expenses incurred in connection with the loan by the government. That, I think, disposes of one of the main bases of the arguments that have been put forward by the speakers for the C.C.F. party in this house this afternoon and this evening.
It is quite understandable, Mr. Speaker, that the C.C.F. party would take this particular position. After all, they are a socialist party; they were against the idea of a pipe line being constructed under private ownership. They believed that this was a field in which public ownership should be called upon to provide these facilities.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES ALLEGED MISLEADING OF PARLIAMENT    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES ALLEGED MISLEADING OF PARLIAMENT    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The government, for perfectly good reasons which still exist, felt that the preferable way was the Canadian traditional method of private enterprise. Obviously, the C.C.F. party from the very beginning have

been against the idea of private risk capital being involved in this project. They therefore have been against the idea of private profit in connection with the project, and they have been consistent in that respect. They are fundamentally against not only the people who have been given and who have exercised options for the purchase of stock making any profit out of the transaction, but they are also on principle against the investors who have invested, in the case of the original investors at $8 a share and in the case of those who have been investing since the public issue at $10 a share, making any profit. As I say, that policy is consistent with their principles.
But, Mr. Speaker, what about the position of the official opposition? I understand they are not a party that lacks confidence in the ordinary workings of the private enterprise system. They are not against the proposition that those who risk their capital in a project of this kind should not, if the project turns out to be a profitable one, reap a reasonable profit that may be coming to them. But the Progressive Conservative party in this house has aligned itself with the proposal of the C.C.F. party in this regard. Their members rose to bring this matter to debate, and it has been supported by a number of speakers from their membership.
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that I believe two of the speakers for the official opposition, the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace, say that the proposal before the house is not what those who propose it say it is but is something different. Well, now, Mr. Speaker, I submit that the proposal before the house and the wording in which it is couched have been pretty carefully thought out and selected by the members of the C.C.F. party to express their views in relation to the way a project of this kind should be handled; and any attempt on the part of the official opposition to say that the wording of this proposal is something different from what it is intended to be, and that they can support it without adopting the basic principles upon which it is founded, is quite erroneous.
The wording shows that they are critical of the fact that some private gain has been possible as a result of the financial support from the public treasury for this project. The Leader of the Opposition has supported the protests of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, and several of his supporters have done the same thing. Mr, Speaker, I do submit that they cannot take this position without the suggestion being quite reasonably made that they are in fact supporting and adopting the socialist principle which is the basis of this motion.
Trans-Canada Pipe Lines
The Minister of Trade and Commerce pointed out what is the basis of the stock option arrangements that Mr. Tanner and Mr. Coates have exercised in accordance with the statements made in the agreement of May 8 and in the other agreements. That is that their investment in this company has not been only a matter of the $8 per share they are undertaking to put up for these shares. There is the additional investment of their energies and abilities, and in fact the dedication of four or five years of their lives to a project which at the time they took it on and during the developmental period while it was being brought to its present state is and for some years in the future will be an investment which provides no certainty of profit at all. These stock options give them an opportunity to reap the benefit of this investment of theirs.
The position of the official opposition apparently is that for some reason or other they do not agree that this system of private enterprise should be permitted to work in this instance. I submit that this is the kind of situation in which the government was wise in trying to have this job done by private enterprise. There is every reason to expect that those who have contributed to and invested in this enterprise either in the form of capital or in the form of service should be given the normal opportunities to make their profit, and that all the profits should not go to those who now are able to come in and put their money into the purchase of stock.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, the suggestion of the motion is that there was something kept from this house and that the house was misled as to some tremendous profit that was going to be made in some hidden way. The motion does not suggest that it was merely a matter of a mistake concerning an unimportant fact; it attacks the whole basis of this arrangement. As far as I am concerned I am quite prepared to let all the socialists in this house-those who are avowed socialists and those who are not-support this position.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES ALLEGED MISLEADING OF PARLIAMENT    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to detain the house very long, and I do not think it is necessary. The first thing that appears to me to be necessary is to consider the terms of the motion that has been offered to Your Honour and which you now have before you. That motion was drafted with five lines in it which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre felt, quite properly I think, should be struck out after the Minister of Trade and Commerce explained today that it was by inadvertence he stated last Tuesday

Trans-Canada Pipe Lines that he was not aware that these options existed. The hon. gentleman said he accepted the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the apology for the mistakes that had been made in the statement of February 19, so that part is not in the motion.
What is in the motion at the present time is a statement that there was signed on behalf of Her Majesty by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, for the government, a contract which contained the statement that there were options for the shares; and that because that kind of contract was signed it is clear that the minister must have been aware of such options when the contract was signed, and in the words of the motion:
. . . hence the need for this house to give consideration to the way in which parliament and the country have been misled by not being informed as to the extent to which there would be private gain as a result of the financial support made available to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited from the public treasury.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the contract was signed on May 8 and was tabled in the house on May 9. Hon. gentlemen have been curious to know whether colleagues of the Minister of Trade and Commerce were aware that options existed. They certainly were aware that options existed, just as all those who looked at the documents which was tabled on May 9 were aware that the options existed. Hon. gentlemen say that for some reason or other they did not see fit to ask what was the extent of the options and at what price they had been given. That no doubt is because they considered at that time, as we considered at that time, that that question was of very little importance. At that time the question was whether or not a pipe line would be built by private enterprise.
The members of the C.C.F. party thought it should be a publicly-owned pipe line whereby the government of Canada would have to negotiate with the commission of the government of Alberta to get gas that was already under contract by the producers to the Trans-Canada pipe line, and they would have subjected the government of Canada or an agency of the government of Canada established by it to the jurisdiction of the public utility commissions of the provinces where the gas was going to be distributed. We felt that was undesirable and that if there could be established a pipe line built and exploited by private enterprise it would be much preferable not to have the government of Canada or an agency of the government of Canada subject to a producers' commission such as exists in Alberta to control the exportation from that province of that

gas, and subject to the public utilities commissions of the provinces where the gas would be distributed.
Personally I felt that if we had been put into that position in order to have the use of this gas in eastern Canada it would have resulted in losses for the government of Canada. There would have been constant pressure for an increase in the price to the producers, who were heard to complain and whose complaints were voiced in this house that the prices they were being offered were insufficient to cover their costs of the producers. There certainly would have been the same kind of protests against the costs to the consumers just as we constantly hear -perhaps with some justification-about the burden of the freight charges that have to be collected by the Canadian National Railways for the transportation of freight.
It would have been an extremely difficult and uncomfortable position for any Canadian government, and I am not at all confident that it would not have resulted in substantial losses for the taxpayers of Canada. In any event we decided that if we could get a pipe line built and exploited by private enterprise it was desirable to have it done in that way. We know there were options outstanding on shares of this company. There are ten million common shares in the stock of this company, and 1,928,183 had been subscribed and paid for at $8 a share.

speechtext:
That was merely for the purpose of incorporating the company and setting it up; but the original shares, the 1,927,181, were sold at $8 per share, and there were options for 60,000 shares to Mr. Tanner and 50,000 shares to Mr. Coates at the same price of $8 per share. At the time no one could inform the house that there were going to be profits and gains as the result of any financial support that was to be given to the company to enable it to get started, and to get the kind of contracts that were necessary to complete the financing of this pipe line.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce asserted from the start that as soon as it was demonstrated to the producers on the one hand, and to the prospective consumers on the

other hand, that the line was going to be built and that financing had been arranged for it or was being arranged for it, there would be no lack of signatories both for the supply of gas in Alberta and for the purchase of gas along the line. That is what has happened.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce was also satisfied that there were such assurances that that would happen, that the money being advanced for the construction of the section across the prairies would be repaid before March 31, 1957-and we are informed that it will be repaid before March 31, 1957-and that the objective of getting the line built and exploited by private enterprise will be realized for the benefit of the Canadian public, and it will be a great contributing factor to industrial development and at the same time the comfort of the people of Canada.
That will have been done because we had sufficient confidence in the future of this country to take whatever risk there was in making that advance and in counting upon the fact that with something which seems almost uncanny to many the Minister of Trade and Commerce has frequently been right in the predictions he has made relating to industrial development. I hope it is not disappointing to anyone to know that the money advanced is going to be returned with interest not later than tomorrow. I would hope there would be none who would feel that that was going to be of such political disadvantage to them, although it was of advantage to the Canadian economy, it is something that should be regretted.
With respect to the number of shares involved in these options, 110,000 against 10,000,000 they represent a little over 1 per cent of the capital stock. If this company can be administered and can serve the Canadian people without there being any other involvement than the involvement resulting from the building by the government of Canada and the government of Ontario of the northern Ontario section, and leasing it at a price which will cover interest and amortization with an option to the company to purchase whenever it is prepared to pay every cent that will have been disbursed by either government, I think that will be of lasting benefit to the Canadian people.
One might have suspected, although suspicions are not things that should be entertained, that because two parties in this house had vigorously opposed everything tending to place this agency in the position where it could build this pipe line, they felt that because there was an election coming on it would be preferable to have attention focused bn these so-called paper profits that may be 82715-1041

speechtext: I rise on a question of privilege. The Prime Minister hopes that the motives which he has just imputed are not the case. Then why did he say what he did? Is he in order in imputing motives? My point of order is that the Prime Minister has imputed to us motives concerning the issue that we raised today which I submit are incorrect. We were prompted to raise this issue today, first because the Minister of Trade and Commerce misled us last Tuesday. Our examination of what he said last Tuesday led us to the realization that we had been misled a year ago by not being informed as to the number of these options to purchase; shares. It was because of that misleading of this house that we felt this matter should be dealt with today, and the Prime Minister must accept that as our motive.

Although I do not want to impute motives I do want to suggest that there is no possible connection whatsoever between the price at which these shares were optioned to executives and the fact that there could or should be an increase in old age pensions. There is nothing to demonstrate that these shares could have been sold at any other price than $8 or perhaps $10 with the commissions that had to be allowed, if the options had not been taken up. The original shares have all been issued at this price of $8 a share, and that was, well, just about 19 times as many as were included in the option.
That being the situation I submit quite confidently that the closing lines of this motion are entirely and absolutely contrary to the facts as demonstrated before the house. There has been no lack of information as to the extent to which there will be private gain as a result of the financial support made available to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited from the public treasury. The hon. gentlemen who have spoken from the other side are using what hindsight they may possess now because of the flurry that took place when these shares were put on the market. I hope there will not be any substantial recession in the price of these shares.
The hon. gentleman can laugh, but unfortunately there are a great many people who have had no occasion to laugh, after having been illusioned by the flurry that took place after an issue that was oversubscribed, in the light of the subsiding which very shortly followed that flurry.
There is no firm determination yet of what these shares are worth. An hon. gentleman, one of the hon. members for Calgary who has had some experience in the organization and operations of petroleum companies, told us he hoped that in the long pull, after some five years, this company will be able to begin paying dividends. I hope it may not be as long as five years, because the economic development of this country is proceeding quite rapidly; but whatever time it may take, there can be no certainty that in a short period there will be a continued demand for these shares at anything more than the original subscribers will have paid for them.

speechtext:
1.	How many persons in Canada received immunization injections of Salk vaccine in 1956?
2.	What was the incidence of reported cases of anterior poliomyelitis among the immunized and non-immunized groups in the same period?
3.	How much Salk vaccine will be available throughout Canada in 1957?
Answer by: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of
National Health and Welfare):
1.	By the summer of 1956 some 1,800,000 children across Canada had received Salk polio vaccine without charge under the national health program. It is expected that by the end of the current fiscal year (March 31, 1957) an additional 1,000,000 children will have been vaccinated, bringing the total to 2,800,000. A very substantial proportion of these children will have received two or more doses of the vaccine.
2.	During 1956, Canada was again fortunate in having an exceptionally small number of cases of poliomyelitis. It will be recalled that in 1955 we had the lowest rate reported in 10 years, with 1,021 cases of all forms of polio, of which 551 were paralytic. Provisional figures for 1956 indicate a total of only 602 cases of all forms of polio, including 361 paralytic cases. When these figures are compared with the t average for the preceding five years they are even more striking. Polio cases of all forms in 1956 were only 15 per cent of the five-year average, while paralytic cases in 1956 amounted to but 23 per cent of this average.
Preliminary figures from nine provinces indicate that during 1956 paralytic poliomyelitis occurred in only 10 children who had received vaccine. A total of 158 cases of paralytic poliomyelitis were reported among all children under 15 years of age in these provinces during the same period. No child who had received all three doses of vaccine

Questions
developed paralytic poliomyelitis, nor were there any polio deaths among vaccinated children.
Although wide annual variations in the number of polio cases have been observed over the years, there is good reason to hope that the extension of the immunization program will exert a progressively beneficial influence in the reduction of the occurrence of paralytic polio.
3.	It is not possible at this time to give a precise answer to this question. The federal government is at present continuing to share 50 per cent of the cost of all vaccine used in provincial immunization programs. Provincial needs for vaccine call for substantial quantities yet to be produced and the utilization of the vaccine will depend upon the ability of the provinces to develop their respective programs. Continuing production will in all likelihood be more than sufficient to enable the provinces to achieve their objective of bringing the total number of vaccinated children to 4,000,000 by the end of the fiscal year 1957-58.

POLIO VACCINE AVAILABILITY AND EXPORT
speechtext:
1.	Has polio vaccine been available for use by practising physicians in Canada?
2.	Is consideration being given to the export of surplus vaccine manufactured in Canada?
Answer by: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of
National Health and Welfare):
1.	All Canadian-produced vaccine has been absorbed in the federal-provincial immunization program. However, to date three commercial manufacturers in the United States have been licensed to distribute Salk polio vaccine in Canada. All imported vaccine has been subjected to the same rigid safety and potency tests in the federal laboratory of hygiene as Canadian-produced vaccine. 2.	While at present there is no surplus of Canadian-manufactured vaccine, it appears likely that continuing production will become more than sufficient to meet provincial requirements. Thus consideration is being given to permitting the export of Canadian-produced vaccine to assist other countries in their efforts to protect children against polio, particularly where critical situations are being encountered. Before any recommendation is made in this respect however it will be assured that the total requirements of each province will be fulfilled, as determined by the availability of personnel and facilities for the administration of the vaccine. This will not be fully apparent for some time but in co-operation with provincial health authorities, officers of the Department of National Health and Welfare are conducting a survey of the situation to determine the most appropriate time to permit surplus Canadian-manufactured vaccine to be made available to others where there may be a demonstrated health need.
